a: As he came down from the mountain
t: Down from the mountain, like Moses
p: Jesus went up the mountain to teach (5:1) and now comes down to act, as Moses came down from Sinai.
b: The Greek almost repeats the Greek Old Testament's words for Moses coming down from Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:29). Matthew has just given Jesus' teaching on a mountain (5:1–7:29); now come his deeds. Two nearly identical summaries frame the section: Jesus teaching, preaching and healing "every kind of disease and illness" (4:23 and 9:35). Between them stand the Sermon on the Mount and ten mighty works. Scholars often call this pair "the Messiah of the word" (chapters 5–7) and "the Messiah of the deed" (chapters 8–9). The crowds that heard the sermon (7:28) now follow him down the hill.

a: a man with a skin disease
p: The Greek lepros means someone with the scaly skin disease of Leviticus 13, not Hansen's disease.
b: Lepros is the Greek Old Testament's word for a person with tsara'at, the skin disease of Leviticus 13–14, which this site renders "skin disease." It covered many flaking or spreading conditions, and even mold in cloth and houses. Modern leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a different illness that may not have reached the Middle East until after Alexander the Great. The problem in the Law was impurity, not contagion: the person lived outside the camp, wore torn clothes and called out "Unclean!" (Leviticus 13:45–46). So the man asks to be made "clean," not just cured. Healing such a person was counted as rare as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7). Parallels: Mark 1:40–45; Luke 5:12–16.
r: Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–32; Numbers 12:10–15; 2 Kings 5:1–14; 2 Kings 5:7; Mark 1:40–45; Luke 5:12–16; 11:5

p: The verb proskyneō can mean kneeling to a superior or worshiping God. Matthew uses it often of Jesus.
b: Proskyneō means to bow or kneel before someone, as subjects did before a king, and also to worship God (4:10). Mark has the man "kneeling" (Mark 1:40). Matthew prefers the stronger word and uses it again and again for those who come to Jesus: the magi (2:2, 11), the official (9:18), the Canaanite woman (15:25), the disciples in the boat (14:33) and after the resurrection (28:9, 17). Inside the story the man shows deep respect. For Matthew's readers, who worshiped Jesus, the word carried more. The same double sense sits in "Lord" (kyrie), which could mean "sir" but in Matthew is the address of faith.

t: A touch that crossed the line
p: Touching a person with skin disease made you unclean. Here the cleanness flows the other way.
b: Under the Law, touching an unclean person made you unclean until evening (Leviticus 5:3; compare Numbers 5:2). Uncleanness was not sin: it was a condition that kept a person from the Temple and was removed by washing, waiting and offerings. Jesus could have healed by a word, as he does in 8:8–13. He touches first, and instead of the impurity passing to him, the cleanness passes to the man. Some older Christian writing pictured purity laws as cruel rules Jesus came to abolish. Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen have pushed back: Jesus does not break the purity system here, since he sends the man to the priest at once (8:4), and nobody in the story objects to the touch.

a: Be careful not to say a word to anyone
p: Jesus often tells the people he heals not to tell. Scholars have long debated why.
b: Jesus gives this order again in 9:30, 12:16 and 16:20. In 1901 William Wrede called it the "messianic secret" and argued that Mark invented it to explain why Jesus was not recognized as Messiah during his life. Most scholars now think the explanation is simpler. (1) Jesus avoided crowds who wanted a wonder-worker or a war leader (compare John 6:15). (2) The healed man had to go to the priest first; news could wait for the Law to be kept. (3) Matthew himself gives the reason in 12:16–21: Jesus is the quiet Servant of Isaiah 42:1–4, who, as Matthew renders it, "will not argue, and he will not shout" (12:19). Here the man does not disobey, as he does in Mark 1:45; Matthew simply moves on.

a: Then bring the gift Moses ordered, as evidence to them
p: Leviticus 14 set out a week-long ritual for a cleansed person. Jesus sends the man to keep it.
b: The "gift" is the offering of Leviticus 14: two birds, then after a week three lambs (or, for the poor, one lamb and two birds), with flour and oil. Only a priest could declare the man clean and let him back into the community and the Temple. Jesus keeps the Law of Moses here, which fits 5:17. "As evidence to them" (eis martyrion autois) can mean: (1) proof to the priests, or to the people, that the man is clean; (2) a witness that Jesus honors the Law; or (3) a witness against them if they do not believe. The same phrase returns in 10:18 and 24:14.

p: A fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, in Herod Antipas's territory.
b: Jesus moved from Nazareth to Capernaum (4:13), and Matthew calls it "his own town" (9:1). It was a town of perhaps a thousand or fifteen hundred people on the lake shore, near the border with Herod Philip's territory, which explains a tax office (9:9) and soldiers. Visitors today see a white limestone synagogue of the 300s or 400s AD built on dark basalt foundations that some excavators date to the first century, and a house venerated from early times as Peter's (see 8:14). Later Jesus pronounces a woe on the town for not repenting (11:23–24).

p: Rome had no legions in Galilee then. He was most likely an officer in Herod Antipas's army, and a Gentile.
b: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, until AD 39, and no Roman legion was stationed there before the war of 66–70. So this officer probably served in Antipas's small army, which was organized on the Roman model and probably drew many of its men from non-Jewish towns. The story assumes he is a Gentile (8:10–11). Luke's version adds that he loved the Jewish people and built their synagogue, and that he sent Jewish elders to ask for him (Luke 7:1–10). John 4:46–54 tells a similar story of a royal official whose son is healed at Capernaum, from Cana. Matthew's centurion is the first of several Gentiles in the Gospel who show faith (15:21–28; 27:54).

p: The Greek pais can mean boy, son or servant. Luke says slave; John's similar story says son.
b: Pais means "child" or "boy," and, like the old English "boy," was also used for a slave or servant of any age. In 8:9 the centurion uses a different word, doulos, "slave," for the one who does what he says. Luke 7:2 calls the sick man a doulos; John's similar story calls him a son (John 4:46). So some read "my boy" as "my son", and most read "my servant." In 2004 Theodore Jennings and Tat-siong Benny Liew argued that pais here meant a younger male partner, as it sometimes did in Greek love poetry. D. B. Saddington replied that nothing in Matthew's or Luke's wording points that way, and most scholars agree with him.

a: I myself will come and heal him.
t: A promise, or a surprised question?
p: The Greek has no question mark and an emphatic "I." Many read it as a question: "Am I to come?"
b: The oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, so translators must decide. The emphatic egō ("I") at the start leads many scholars, among them Davies and Allison and R. T. France, to read a question: "Am I to come and heal him?" A Jew who entered a Gentile's house could become unclean; later the Mishnah says the dwellings of Gentiles are unclean (Mishnah Oholot 18:7), and Peter needs a vision before he enters Cornelius's house (Acts 10:28). On this reading Jesus tests the man, as he later tests the Canaanite woman (15:21–28), and the centurion's answer, "I am not good enough for you to come in," fits well. Others, following the older versions, take it as a ready promise. The Plain keeps the statement but marks the "I" as strong.
orig: Ἐγὼ ἐλθὼν θεραπεύσω αὐτόν (egō elthōn therapeusō auton)

a: I am not good enough for you to come in under my roof
p: Churches still borrow the centurion's words just before receiving Communion.
b: Hikanos means "fit" or "good enough." The centurion's humility became one of the best-known prayers in Christian worship. In the Roman Catholic Mass, the people say a form of his words just before Communion, with "my soul" in place of "my servant." Many Anglican and Lutheran orders of service use similar words. Augustine and Chrysostom praised the man as a model of humility: he thought himself unworthy to have Jesus in his house, and so, Augustine said (Sermon 62), he received Jesus into his heart. His faith rests on the power of Jesus' word: "Only say a word."

p: The Greek doulos means a slave, owned by another. Many English Bibles soften it to "servant."
b: This is the first time Matthew uses doulos. In the Roman world a slave was property: bought, sold, and without legal rights, though slaves did every kind of work, from farm labor to managing estates. A centurion would likely own one or more. Older English Bibles often said "servant," partly because "slave" called up the very different race-based slavery of the Americas. This site says "slave" for doulos, as in Jude 1:1, and "servant" for other words. The centurion's point: he is under orders and gives orders, and his word is obeyed at a distance. He believes Jesus' word works the same way over sickness.

a: I have not met faith this great in anyone in Israel
p: The first person in Matthew whom Jesus praises for great faith is a Gentile soldier.
b: On only two occasions do the Gospels say Jesus was "amazed": here (with Luke's parallel, Luke 7:9), at faith, and in Mark 6:6, at unbelief. Matthew sets the Gentile officer beside Jesus' own people: the next Gentile praised for "great faith" is the Canaanite woman (15:28). This does not mean no Jew had faith. In this same section a leper, a paralyzed man's friends, an official, a bleeding woman and two blind men, all Jews, come in faith. The point is surprise: true faith shows up where no one expected it. Matthew's mostly Jewish-Christian readers, already welcoming Gentiles (28:19), would have heard their own story in it.

a: many will come from the sunrise and the sunset
p: Most read Gentiles coming to God's feast. Some scholars think Jews scattered abroad are meant.
b: The prophets pictured people streaming to God from east and west, sometimes the nations (Isaiah 2:2–3; Isaiah 45:6; Malachi 1:11), sometimes scattered Israel coming home (Isaiah 43:5–6; Psalm 107:3; Zechariah 8:7–8). (1) Most interpreters, ancient and modern, read Gentiles here: the centurion is the first of many. (2) Davies and Allison argue the "many" are Jews of the dispersion, who will share the feast while some Jews of the land are shut out; the saying in itself does not mention Gentiles. Luke places the saying elsewhere and adds north and south (Luke 13:28–29), which suggests it once circulated on its own. In Matthew's setting, with a Gentile's faith just praised, the first reading is the natural one.
r: Isaiah 2:2–3; Isaiah 25:6–8; Isaiah 43:5–6; Isaiah 49:12; Malachi 1:11; Psalm 107:3; Luke 13:28–29; 22:1–14

a: lie down to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: Guests at a feast lay on couches. The end of the age is pictured as a dinner with the patriarchs.
b: At formal dinners people reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow. The image of the age to come as a feast goes back to Isaiah 25:6–8, where the LORD prepares a banquet "for all peoples" on his mountain and swallows up death. Later Jewish writings developed it (1 Enoch 62:14 has the righteous eating with the Son of Man), and Jesus uses it again in the wedding parables (22:1–14; 25:10) and at the Last Supper (26:29). The patriarchs are present because the dead will be raised (22:31–32). Eating with someone meant accepting them, which is why Jesus' meals with sinners cause such offense (9:10–11).

t: Who are "the sons of the kingdom"?
p: Those who should have been the heirs. In 13:38 the same phrase means Jesus' faithful followers.
b: "Sons of" is a Hebrew way to say "those who belong to." Here the phrase means those who expected to inherit the kingdom, in context people of Israel who reject Jesus. It is a prophetic warning in the style of John the Baptist (3:9) and Amos (Amos 3:2), not a verdict on a race. In 13:38 "the sons of the kingdom" are the good seed, Jesus' followers, and Matthew warns his own church just as sharply (7:21–23; 22:11–14; 25:30). Christians later read verses like this as "the Jews are thrown out and the church replaces them," a reading that fed contempt for Jews. Many churches have since rejected that reading (see the note at 21:43 and the topic page).

a: There people will weep and grind their teeth
p: Matthew's signature phrase for final loss. It appears six times in this Gospel and once in Luke.
b: The phrase is almost Matthew's own: 8:12; 13:42; 13:50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30 (and once in Luke 13:28). Grinding the teeth can be anger (Psalm 35:16; Psalm 112:10; Acts 7:54) or anguish. "The darkness outside" (literally "the outer darkness") pictures a lit banquet hall at night, with the shut-out guest standing in the dark (22:13; 25:30). The images describe exclusion and regret. How literally they describe a place of punishment is debated (see 10:28).

p: Peter was married. Excavators found a house in Capernaum honored as his from early times.
b: Peter had a wife, who later traveled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5). Excavations at Capernaum since 1968 uncovered a modest house of basalt rooms around courtyards. One room was plastered and set apart for gatherings, apparently by Christians, possibly as early as the late first century, with later graffiti naming Jesus and Peter. In the 400s an eight-sided church was built over it. A pilgrim of the late 300s, Egeria, wrote that Peter's house in Capernaum had been made into a church. Most archaeologists think the identification is plausible though not proved. Parallels: Mark 1:29–31; Luke 4:38–39.

p: The verb diakoneō is the root of "deacon." Matthew has her serve Jesus himself.
b: In Mark she serves "them" (Mark 1:31). Matthew narrows it to "him," and the scene becomes a small call story: Jesus sees, touches, she rises, and she serves him, just as he "saw" Matthew and called him (9:9). The verb diakoneō is used of angels serving Jesus (4:11), of Jesus himself, who came to serve, not to be served (20:28), and of the women who followed him from Galilee "serving him" (27:55). "Got up" (ēgerthē) is also the verb for resurrection (28:6).

a: He himself took our weaknesses and carried our diseases.
p: Matthew quotes the Suffering Servant song, translating the Hebrew directly, about bodily sickness.
b: Isaiah 53:4 in Hebrew speaks of the Servant bearing ḥoli (sickness) and mak'ov (pain). The Greek Old Testament made it spiritual: "he bears our sins and suffers pain for us." Matthew instead gives a fresh, close rendering of the Hebrew and applies it to Jesus' healings, not to his death. Readers have argued over what follows. Pentecostal and Holiness teachers such as A. B. Simpson taught that healing is "in the atonement": Christ bore sickness as he bore sin, so believers may claim healing now. Many other interpreters reply that Matthew applies the verse to Jesus' healing ministry before the cross, and that full healing awaits the resurrection. See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter.

p: In Matthew outsiders call Jesus "Teacher"; disciples and people of faith call him "Lord."
b: Scholars have noticed a pattern. In Matthew, disciples and people who come in faith address Jesus as "Lord" (8:2, 6, 21, 25; 9:28), while scribes, Pharisees and others call him "Teacher" (12:38; 19:16; 22:16, 24, 36). At the Last Supper the eleven ask, "Surely not I, Lord?" but Judas asks, "Surely not I, Rabbi?" (26:22, 25). So the scribe's polite title may already hint that he has not grasped who Jesus is. Others note that being a teacher's follower was normal in Judaism, and the scribe's offer is sincere; Jesus simply tells him the cost.

t: The Son of Man: first use in Matthew
p: Jesus' favorite way of naming himself. It can mean simply "a human being," or point to Daniel 7.
b: This is the first of about thirty times in Matthew. Only Jesus uses it, always of himself. In Hebrew and Aramaic, "son of man" (ben adam, bar enash) means "a human being" (Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1). In Daniel 7:13 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds and receives a kingdom, and the Parables of Enoch (1 Enoch 46–71) make the Son of Man a heavenly judge. Scholars debate how Jesus used it: Geza Vermes argued it was an Aramaic way of saying "I"; many others see a title drawn from Daniel. Jesus' sayings fall in three groups: his life on earth (as here, homeless), his suffering (17:22), and his future coming (10:23; 26:64).
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

a: Let the dead bury their own dead
p: Burying a father was one of the most sacred duties. Readers have tried several ways to explain it.
b: Burying parents fulfilled the command to honor them; Tobit risks his life to bury the dead (Tobit 1:17–19; Tobit 4:3), and the Mishnah frees a mourner whose dead lies unburied from saying the Shema (Mishnah Berakhot 3:1). Readings: (1) The spiritually dead can bury the physically dead; following Jesus comes first (most interpreters since the fathers). (2) The father was not yet dead: "Let me first bury my father" meant "let me stay home until he dies." (3) Byron McCane argued it refers to the second burial a year later, when bones were gathered into a bone box. (4) Martin Hengel saw a deliberate shock, like the prophets forbidden to mourn (Jeremiah 16:5–7; Ezekiel 24:15–18): the call of the kingdom outranks even the holiest duty.
r: Tobit 4:3; Tobit 1:17–19; Exodus 20:12; 1 Kings 19:19–21; Jeremiah 16:5–7; Ezekiel 24:15–18; Leviticus 21:11; Luke 9:59–60; 10:37

a: a great storm shook the sea
p: Matthew's word is seismos, "shaking," the word he uses for the earthquakes at the cross and the tomb.
b: Mark and Luke call it a squall of wind (Mark 4:37; Luke 8:23). Matthew writes seismos megas, "a great shaking," the word for earthquake. He uses it again for the end-time troubles (24:7) and for the earthquakes at Jesus' death and resurrection (27:54; 28:2). The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level among hills, and sudden violent winds still sweep down on it. Matthew calls the lake "the sea" (thalassa), and for Israel the sea was the image of chaos that only God can master (Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:23–30).

t: Asleep in the storm, like Jonah
p: Jonah also slept in a ship during a great storm, until the frightened crew woke him.
b: The story echoes Jonah 1: a great storm, a sleeping man, terrified sailors who wake him, a calm sea and amazed men. The difference is the point: Jonah was running from God and had to be thrown in; Jesus speaks and the sea obeys. Matthew later makes the link to Jonah himself: "here is something greater than Jonah" (12:41). Sleep in a storm also shows trust in God (Psalm 3:5; Psalm 4:8), while in the psalms God is sometimes called on to "wake up" and help (Psalm 44:23).

p: Since Günther Bornkamm (1948) many read Matthew's version as a picture of the church in trouble.
b: In Mark the disciples say, "Teacher... doesn't it matter to you that we are going down?" (Mark 4:38). Matthew's disciples "follow" him into the boat (8:23, the discipleship word, after 8:19–22), call him "Lord" and pray, "Lord, save," the language of worship (compare 14:30). Jesus speaks to their "little faith" before he calms the sea. Günther Bornkamm argued that Matthew shaped the story into a lesson for his church, tossed in persecution, with the Lord present though he seems asleep. Early Christians drew the same picture: Tertullian calls the boat in the storm a figure of the church. Others think the details simply reflect Matthew's tidier style.

p: Oligopistoi is almost a word Matthew coined. It means weak trust, not no faith at all.
b: Matthew uses oligopistos four times (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8) and the noun once (17:20); Luke has it once (Luke 12:28). In Mark the question is harsher: "Why are you timid? You still don't have faith?" (Mark 4:40). Matthew's disciples have faith, but it fails under pressure. Note the order too: Jesus speaks to the disciples' fear first, then to the storm.

a: even the winds and the sea do what he says
p: In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something only God does.
b: The psalms praise God in just these terms: "You are master of the sea when it swells" (Psalm 89:9; compare Psalm 65:7; Psalm 107:29; Job 38:8–11). The men's question, "What sort of person is this?", is left open for the reader. Matthew answers it later, when the disciples in another storm bow down and call him the Son of God (14:33).

p: Mark and Luke tell of one man. Matthew often has two where the others have one.
b: Mark 5:1–20 and Luke 8:26–39 have one man, named Legion. Matthew has two here, two blind men in 9:27–31 and 20:29–34 (Mark has one, Bartimaeus), and two animals at the entry to Jerusalem (21:2–7). Explanations: (1) Augustine: there were two, but one was better known, so Mark and Luke mention only him. (2) Matthew wants two witnesses, as the Law requires (Deuteronomy 19:15). (3) Matthew combines stories, here perhaps making up for skipping Mark's exorcism in the Capernaum synagogue (Mark 1:23–28). Matthew's version is also much shorter: no name, no chains, no man begging to follow Jesus.

a: came out from among the tombs
p: Everything here was unclean for a Jew: Gentile territory, tombs, pigs and demons.
b: The east shore of the lake belonged to the Decapolis, a league of Greek cities. Tombs made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16), and pigs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:7), raised here for the Greek market. Isaiah 65:4 describes people "who sit in tombs" and "eat the flesh of pigs" as a rebellious people, and some think the story echoes it. Jesus crosses into the most unclean place imaginable, and the unclean spirits are the ones who must leave.

a: What is there between us and you
p: A Hebrew idiom that pushes someone away: "What do we have in common?" or "Leave us alone."
b: The Greek copies a Hebrew phrase, literally "What to us and to you?" It says the two parties have nothing in common, or asks why one is interfering with the other (Judges 11:12; 2 Samuel 16:10; 1 Kings 17:18; 2 Kings 3:13; Mark 1:24; John 2:4). Spoken by demons, it is hostile and afraid. They also know who Jesus is, "Son of God," the title the devil used in the testing (4:3, 6). "Ahead of time" assumes a set time of judgment for evil spirits, a common Jewish belief (1 Enoch 16:1; Jubilees 10:8–9). Jesus' exorcisms show that the end has broken in early (12:28).
orig: Τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί (ti hēmin kai soi)
r: Judges 11:12; 2 Samuel 16:10; 1 Kings 17:18; John 2:4; Mark 1:24; 4:3; 4:6; 1 Enoch 16:1; Jubilees 10:8–9; 12:28; Revelation 20:10

a: Then the whole herd charged down the cliff into the sea
p: Readers since antiquity have asked why Jesus allowed the herd to be destroyed.
b: The question is old. Bertrand Russell listed the drowned pigs among his objections to Jesus' character (1927). Answers given: (1) The demons, not Jesus, destroy the pigs; evil ruins whatever it enters, and the story shows what the demons wanted to do to the men. (2) The rush into the sea proves to everyone that the men are truly free. (3) The sea was the home of chaos, and the evil goes back to the deep (compare Revelation 20:10, and Luke 8:31, "the abyss"). (4) The story shows that one human life is worth more than a herd. The town's answer is the saddest: they ask Jesus to leave (8:34).

p: The Greek present tense says "are being forgiven" now, a divine passive: God is the one forgiving.
b: Aphientai is present tense: forgiveness happens as Jesus speaks. The passive voice was a common Jewish way of speaking of God's action without naming him. Many people then linked sickness and sin (John 9:2; Psalm 103:3; James 5:15), though the Bible also denies a simple link (Job; John 9:3). Jesus sees "their faith," the faith of the friends who carried the man, not only his own. A Dead Sea Scroll, the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), has a Babylonian king say that a Jewish exorcist "forgave my sin" and healed him, so Jews could picture a healer announcing forgiveness. Parallels: Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26.
orig: ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι (aphientai sou hai hamartiai)
r: Psalm 103:3; Psalm 32:1–5; Isaiah 33:24; James 5:15; John 9:2–3; Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26

p: The scribes think Jesus claims what belongs to God. Later Jewish law defined blasphemy more narrowly.
b: Mark spells out the scribes' thought: "Who is able to forgive sins except the one God?" (Mark 2:7). Matthew leaves it implied. Under the Law, blasphemy, cursing God's name, was a capital crime (Leviticus 24:15–16). The Mishnah, compiled about AD 200, says a blasphemer is guilty only if he pronounces the divine name itself (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5), which Jesus does not do here. In the first century the term was probably looser, covering any insult to God's honor. The same charge returns at Jesus' trial before the high priest (26:65), so this first conflict foreshadows the last.

a: the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins here on earth
p: The crowd praises God for giving such authority "to people," plural. What does that mean?
b: Jesus links his healing word to his forgiving word: the healing that people can see proves the forgiveness they cannot. "On earth" contrasts with heaven, where God forgives. In 9:8 the crowds praise God for giving such authority "to human beings" (plural). Readings: (1) The crowd simply means Jesus, a man (a general plural). (2) Matthew hints that Jesus shares this authority with his followers, who will "bind and loose" (16:19; 18:18) and are taught to forgive (6:12–15; 18:21–35). Catholic and Orthodox readers have seen here the root of the church's ministry of absolution; Protestant readers usually see the church's proclaiming of forgiveness. See the card on this chapter.

p: The crowd's "fear" is awe before God's power, which turns into praise.
b: Phobeomai covers both terror and reverent awe. In the Bible, fear is the natural human response when God acts nearby (17:6; 27:54; 28:8), and it often leads to worship. Here it turns at once into praise: they "glorified God." Many later manuscripts have "they were amazed" instead (see the variant), probably because fear seemed an odd reaction to a healing.

p: Mark and Luke tell the same story about "Levi." Only this Gospel calls the tax collector Matthew.
b: In Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 the man at the tax booth is Levi son of Alphaeus. All three Gospels list a Matthew among the Twelve, but only this Gospel calls him "Matthew the tax collector" (10:3). Views: (1) One man with two names, like Simon Peter (a common traditional view). (2) The Gospel's author, by church tradition the apostle Matthew, is quietly signing his own story. (3) Many critical scholars think the writer, using Mark, changed the name so that the call story would belong to one of the Twelve, since Levi is not in any list. The name Matthew (Hebrew Mattityahu) means "gift of the LORD." See the book's introduction on authorship.

t: A toll booth on the border
p: Capernaum sat near the border between the lands of Herod Antipas and his brother Philip.
b: The telōnion was a toll or customs booth. Goods passing between Herod Philip's territory and Herod Antipas's Galilee, or landed by boats on the lake, paid duty. Rulers sold the right to collect such tolls to contractors, who hired local agents and kept anything they could collect above the contract. So a Galilean toll collector worked for Antipas, and through him for a system that served Rome. That is why such men were seen as greedy collaborators.

p: Not ordinary people who missed a ritual, most scholars now think, but people known for flouting God's law.
b: Tax collectors were scorned: the Mishnah allows a man to lie to a tax collector, as to a robber or murderer (Mishnah Nedarim 3:4), and says a house becomes unclean if tax collectors enter it (Mishnah Tohorot 7:6). Joachim Jeremias argued that "sinners" meant the common people, the am ha'arets, whom strict Pharisees looked down on for not keeping purity rules. E. P. Sanders replied that "sinners" in Jewish usage meant the wicked, people who broke the commandments and did not repent. On his reading the offense was not that Jesus ate with ordinary folk but that he welcomed the wicked before they had made restitution.

p: Many Pharisees took care over what they ate and with whom. Sharing a table meant sharing a life.
b: The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law and the traditions of their teachers (see the note at 3:7). Jacob Neusner argued that their main concern in Jesus' day was eating ordinary meals in the purity required of priests, and so choosing table companions carefully; Sanders and others think this is overstated. Either way, in that culture a meal was not neutral. To eat with someone was to accept them. The Pharisees ask the disciples, not Jesus. In Matthew's day, after AD 70, the heirs of the Pharisees led the synagogues that Matthew's church argued with, which colors how Matthew tells these scenes.

a: Go and find out what this means
p: "Go and learn" echoes a phrase rabbis used to send a student back to the text.
b: The Hebrew formula tse u-lemad, "go and learn," appears in later rabbinic teaching when a teacher points a student to a verse. Jesus turns the Pharisees, experts in the Law, back to their own Scriptures. Matthew alone has this quotation, and he uses it twice (here and 12:7), both times against critics who put a rule above a person in need.

a: 'Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice.'
p: Hosea's words, in Matthew alone, twice. The Hebrew word is hesed, loyal love.
b: In Hosea 6:6 God says, "I desire loyal love (hesed) and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings." The Greek Old Testament rendered hesed as eleos, "mercy," which Matthew quotes. The "not ... but" is a Hebrew way of saying "this matters more than that"; the prophets did not reject the Temple, they rejected worship without justice (1 Samuel 15:22; Micah 6:6–8). After the Temple fell in AD 70, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai is said to have comforted a student with this very verse: acts of loving-kindness atone as sacrifice did (Avot de-Rabbi Nathan A 4). Jesus and the rabbis both made Hosea 6:6 central.
orig: Ἔλεος θέλω καὶ οὐ θυσίαν (eleos thelō kai ou thysian)

a: I did not come to call righteous people
p: Jesus may be speaking with irony, or simply saying who his mission is for.
b: Readings: (1) Irony: those who think they are righteous do not see their need. (2) Plain sense: some people really are on God's path (1:19; 5:20), and a doctor goes to the sick, not the healthy. (3) A statement of mission: Jesus came to call, invite, those whom others had given up on, as at a banquet (22:9). "Call" (kaleō) is also the word for inviting guests to a meal (22:3–9), which fits the dinner setting.

a: We fast a great deal, and so do the Pharisees
p: Pious Jews fasted on set days. The Didache later told Christians to fast on different days.
b: The Law commanded only one fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31). Many devout Jews added more. The Pharisee in Luke's parable fasts "twice a week" (Luke 18:12), and the Didache, an early Christian manual, tells believers not to fast on Monday and Thursday "with the hypocrites" but on Wednesday and Friday (Didache 8:1), showing that Jews then fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. John the Baptist's disciples lived strictly, like their teacher (3:4; 11:18). Jesus had taught how to fast, not whether (6:16–18). Parallels: Mark 2:18–22; Luke 5:33–39.

p: In the prophets God is Israel's husband. Jesus calls himself the groom, and hints at his death.
b: "Sons of the bridal chamber" is a Hebrew idiom for the groom's attendants, who made the wedding week a celebration; fasting then would be absurd. The prophets pictured God as Israel's bridegroom (Isaiah 54:5; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:16–20). By casting himself as the groom, Jesus makes a large claim, which returns in the parables of the wedding feast and the ten young women (22:1–14; 25:1–13; compare John 3:29; Revelation 19:7). "Taken away" is the first hint in Matthew of his death; the verb is close to Isaiah 53:8 in Greek. Christians fast, Jesus says, in the time after he is gone.
r: Isaiah 54:5; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:16–20; 22:1–14; 25:1–13; John 3:29; Revelation 19:7; Isaiah 53:8

p: Only Matthew adds that both wine and skins are saved. Is the new replacing the old, or keeping it?
b: New wine still fermenting would stretch and split an old, brittle skin. The two images say that what Jesus brings cannot simply be stitched onto old ways. Some early Christians, above all Marcion in the 100s, read this as the gospel discarding the Jewish Scriptures. Matthew alone ends with "both are kept safe": the concern is to preserve, not to destroy. That fits his Jesus, who came "not to do away with them but to fulfill them" (5:17), and his scribe who brings out "new things and old things" (13:52). Many scholars read the saying as Matthew's answer to fellow Jews: following Jesus keeps the Law and the Prophets, in new skins.

p: Mark and Luke name him Jairus, a synagogue leader, and say the girl was dying. In Matthew she has died.
b: Matthew's account is much shorter than Mark 5:21–43 and Luke 8:40–56. He leaves out the name Jairus and the messengers who bring news of the death. Here the father says from the start, "My daughter died just now," which makes his faith bolder: he asks for a raising, not a healing. The father's "bowed down" is the same word as in 8:2. The two stories, a girl of twelve (Mark 5:42) and a woman ill for twelve years, are woven together in all three Gospels. The manuscripts word the official's arrival in several ways: "one official came," "one official came up," "a certain official came in" and others (Tischendorf). The editions here follow "one official came" (archōn heis elthōn), but the English sense does not change.

a: a flow of blood for twelve years
p: Leviticus 15 made such a woman unclean. Jewish scholars warn against overstating her isolation.
b: A woman with a long discharge of blood was unclean, and made unclean whatever she lay or sat on, until seven days after it stopped (Leviticus 15:25–30). Sermons often say she was cut off from family and synagogue and that Jesus broke the Law by letting her touch him. Amy-Jill Levine has pointed out that Matthew says nothing about impurity, that purity laws applied mainly to approaching the Temple, and that Jesus is not made unclean in a way anyone in the story notices. The story's point is her faith and Jesus' power, not a quarrel with the Law. Her twelve years of suffering also cost money and hope (Mark 5:26).

p: Kraspedon is the tassel (tsitsit) that the Law told every Israelite man to wear on his cloak's corners.
b: Numbers 15:38–40 and Deuteronomy 22:12 command tassels on the four corners of the outer garment, with a blue cord, as reminders of God's commands. The Greek Old Testament calls them kraspeda, the word here. So Jesus, as an observant Jew, wore tassels, and the woman reached for one. Others later did the same (14:36), and Jesus criticizes those who make their tassels long for show (23:5). Zechariah 8:23 pictures ten men from the nations taking hold of "the corner" of a Jew's garment, asking to go with him. The KJV's "hem" hides the link.

p: The verb sōzō covers rescue, healing and salvation. Matthew uses it three times in two verses.
b: Sōzō means to rescue, keep safe, heal or save. Most English Bibles split it: "I will be made well... your faith has made you well." The Plain keeps "saved" all three times so the reader can hear what Matthew's readers heard. The name Jesus means "the LORD saves," and the angel said he would "save his people from their sins" (1:21). The disciples in the boat cried, "Lord, save us!" (8:25). For Matthew bodily rescue and salvation are two sides of one work.

p: Even a poor family hired flute players and wailing women for a funeral.
b: Funerals began quickly, often on the day of death, with loud public grief. The Mishnah says that even the poorest man in Israel must provide at least two flute players and one wailing woman when his wife dies (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4). The prophets mention professional mourning women (Jeremiah 9:17–18; Amos 5:16). A crowd "in an uproar" means the mourning had already begun: the girl was really dead, and everyone knew it.
r: Jeremiah 9:17–18; Jeremiah 48:36; Amos 5:16; 2 Chronicles 35:25; Mark 5:38; Luke 8:52

p: Jesus says the girl sleeps. Most read this as a picture of death that he is about to undo.
b: The father says she has died (9:18), and the mourners laugh because they know it. "Sleep" was a common Jewish and Christian picture of death, especially of death that ends in resurrection (Daniel 12:2; John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 27:52). Most interpreters read Jesus as saying her death is like sleep, because he will wake her. A few modern readers have suggested a coma, which Jesus diagnosed; that does not fit Matthew's telling, in which she has plainly died and the deed is listed among the dead raised (11:5).

p: "Rose up" (ēgerthē) is the verb Matthew uses for the raising of the dead and for Jesus' own resurrection.
b: The verb is the same one used in 10:8 ("raise the dead"), 11:5 ("the dead are raised"), 27:52 and of Jesus himself: "He has been raised" (28:6–7). Jesus "took hold of her hand," as he did for Peter's mother-in-law (8:15). The prophets Elijah and Elisha had also raised children (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37), but with long prayer; Jesus simply takes her hand. Matthew does not record the words "Talitha koum" (Mark 5:41).

p: The title means the promised king from David's line. In Matthew it is linked again and again with healing.
b: "Son of David" opens the Gospel (1:1) and means the Messiah promised to David's family (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Strangely, in Matthew it is cried mostly by the blind, the sick and outsiders asking for healing (9:27; 12:23; 15:22; 20:30–31; 21:14–15). Dennis Duling showed that Jewish tradition made David's son Solomon a master of healing and exorcism (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 8.45–49; the Testament of Solomon), which may explain the link. The prophets also promised that in the age to come "blind people's eyes will open" (Isaiah 35:5). Matthew tells a similar story of two blind men near Jericho (20:29–34).

a: Jesus gave them a fierce warning
p: Embrimaomai describes a horse snorting. It shows strong emotion, often anger.
b: The verb is used for snorting with anger or deep feeling (Mark 14:5; John 11:33, 38). Here it shows how strongly Jesus wanted no publicity (see 8:4). The men disobey at once. Matthew does not blame them, but the crowds that follow make Jesus' work harder (compare Mark 1:45).

a: Never has anything like this appeared in Israel!
p: The crowd's cry closes a set of ten miracles, which many scholars think Matthew arranged on purpose.
b: Chapters 8–9 hold ten miracles: the leper, the centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, the storm, the men with demons, the paralyzed man, the official's daughter, the bleeding woman, the two blind men and the man who could not speak. They are grouped in threes, with sayings about discipleship between. Some see a link with the ten plagues by which Moses' God showed his power in Egypt, or with the ten wonders done for Israel at the sea (Mishnah Avot 5:4). Others doubt Matthew counted. The crowd's verdict and the Pharisees' answer (9:34) set up the split that runs through the rest of the Gospel: amazement on one side, hostility on the other.

a: his heart went out to them
p: Splanchnizomai comes from splanchna, the inner organs, where feelings were thought to live.
b: In the Gospels the verb is used of Jesus and of a few figures in his parables: the king and the father who stand for God (18:27; Luke 15:20), and the good Samaritan (Luke 10:33). It translates the deep, bodily pity of the Hebrew rachamim, mother-love, related to rechem, "womb." In Matthew Jesus' compassion leads to action: teaching, healing, feeding and sending (14:14; 15:32; 20:34). Here it leads to the sending of the Twelve.

a: like sheep that have no shepherd
p: Moses prayed that Israel would not be "like sheep without a shepherd," and God gave them Joshua.
b: The phrase comes from Numbers 27:17, where Moses asks God to appoint a leader so the people will not be like shepherdless sheep, and God names Joshua, whose name in Greek is Iēsous, Jesus. It returns in 1 Kings 22:17 and in Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's bad shepherds, promises to search for the lost himself, and sets "my servant David" over them as shepherd (Ezekiel 34:5–6, 23). Matthew has already quoted Micah: a ruler "who will shepherd my people Israel" (2:6). The "lost sheep" of 10:6 follow from here.

p: In the prophets the harvest is the final judgment. Jesus makes it a mission field.
b: The prophets used the harvest for the day of God's judgment (Joel 3:13; Isaiah 27:12; Hosea 6:11), and Matthew does too (3:12; 13:30, 39). Here the image turns: the harvest is people ready to be gathered in, and the problem is too few workers. The "Lord of the harvest" is God. The next verse's verb, "send out" (ekballō, literally "throw out"), is the same verb Jesus uses for driving out demons, which gives the prayer urgency.

p: Twelve stands for the twelve tribes. Jesus is gathering a renewed Israel around himself.
b: Matthew assumes the reader already knows the Twelve; only five of their calls have been told (4:18–22; 9:9). The number echoes the twelve sons of Jacob and twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus will tell them they will "sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel" (19:28). In Jesus' day ten of the tribes had been scattered for centuries, and prophets and later writings hoped God would gather all twelve again (Isaiah 49:6; Ezekiel 37:15–28). E. P. Sanders called the choice of twelve one of the surest signs that Jesus looked for the restoration of Israel. When Judas fell, the church filled his place to keep the number (Acts 1:15–26).
r: 19:28; Genesis 49:28; Isaiah 49:6; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Acts 1:15–26; Revelation 21:12–14; Mark 3:13–19; Luke 6:12–16

p: The only time Matthew uses the word. An apostle is an envoy who carries the sender's authority.
b: Apostolos means "one who is sent," from apostellō, "send out" (10:5, 16). Many scholars compare the Jewish idea of the shaliach, an agent: "A person's agent is like the person himself" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). That is the logic of 10:40: whoever welcomes the messengers welcomes Jesus, and whoever welcomes him welcomes God. Matthew uses the noun only here; elsewhere they are "the twelve disciples" or "the Twelve." Luke and Paul use "apostle" more widely (Luke 6:13; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Romans 16:7).

a: first Simon, the one called Peter
p: Matthew alone adds "first" to Peter's name in the list. First in time, or first in rank?
b: Peter heads every list of the Twelve (Mark 3:16; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13), but only Matthew writes prōtos, "first." Since no "second" or "third" follows, many take it as rank, not counting. Matthew gives Peter a special place: he walks on water (14:28–31), confesses Jesus as Messiah and is called the rock (16:16–19), and pays the Temple tax for both (17:24–27). Catholic readers see a sign of Peter's primacy among the apostles, continued in the bishops of Rome. Orthodox readers grant Peter a primacy of honor. Most Protestants see Peter as first called and spokesman, not as holder of an office handed on. The full debate belongs to 16:18 and its card.

p: The four lists agree on most names but not all. Thaddaeus here is Judas son of James in Luke.
b: The lists in Matthew 10:2–4, Mark 3:16–19, Luke 6:14–16 and Acts 1:13 have the same names in three groups of four, each led by Peter, Philip and James son of Alphaeus. Where Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus, Luke and Acts have "Judas son of James," and John 14:22 mentions "Judas, not Iscariot." Most suppose one man with two names. Bartholomew ("son of Talmai") is a family name; since the 800s many have identified him with Nathanael (John 1:45–49), because John never names Bartholomew and the other Gospels never name Nathanael. Thomas means "twin" (John 11:16). James son of Alphaeus may be related to Levi son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14), but the text does not say.

p: Kananaios comes from the Aramaic for "zealous." Luke translates it "the Zealot."
b: Kananaios is a Greek spelling of the Aramaic qan'ana, "zealot, zealous one"; Luke gives the Greek equivalent, Zēlōtēs (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). The KJV's "Simon the Canaanite" follows the later spelling Kananitēs, which is misleading: in English it suggests the people of Canaan. Jerome took the word to mean "from Cana," but most scholars now trace it to the Aramaic. Whether Simon belonged to the Zealots, the revolutionary party Josephus describes in the war of 66–70, is unclear, since that party may not have formed until then. "Zealous" could also describe zeal for the Law, in the line of Phinehas and the Maccabees (Numbers 25:11; 1 Maccabees 2:24–27). Either way, Jesus chose a zealot and a tax collector for the same group.
r: Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13; Numbers 25:11; 1 Maccabees 2:24–27; Galatians 1:14; Acts 21:20

a: Judas Iscariot, the one who also handed him over
p: "Iscariot" is unexplained. "Handed over" is the same verb used of the disciples' own arrests.
b: Proposed meanings of Iscariot: (1) Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, "man of Kerioth," a town in Judah (Joshua 15:25), which would make Judas the only southerner among the Twelve; John calls his father "Simon Iscariot" (John 6:71). (2) Sicarius, "dagger man," a name for later Jewish rebels. (3) An Aramaic word for "liar" or "false one." The first is most common. The verb paradidōmi, "hand over," is the word for Judas's betrayal (26:15–16), and in this same chapter for the disciples being handed over to courts (10:17, 19, 21). Matthew names the betrayal at the very first mention of Judas.

a: Do not go off on a road to the Gentiles
t: Only to Israel, then to all nations
p: Here Jesus limits the mission to Israel. At the end he sends the Eleven to all nations (28:19).
b: Only Matthew has this command, and Jesus says the same of himself to the Canaanite woman (15:24). Yet the Gospel ends with the command to make disciples of all the nations (28:19). Readings: (1) Two stages: Israel first, then the world after the resurrection, as Paul also says ("to the Jew first," Romans 1:16; Acts 13:46); most commentators. (2) Matthew's community history: the saying comes from an early, Israel-only mission among Jewish Christians, which Matthew keeps while showing it widened. (3) The historical Jesus: Joachim Jeremias argued Jesus himself expected the nations to come to God at the end, as the prophets said, not through missionaries now. (4) Jewish readers often see here a Jesus whose work was a renewal within Israel. Whether 28:19 includes Israel is itself debated. Many hold that "all the nations" includes the Jewish people, so 10:6 is widened, not cancelled; Douglas Hare and Daniel Harrington (1975) argued that it means the Gentiles, so that the mission to Israel had ended in Matthew's eyes.

p: The people of Samaria worshiped the God of Israel at Mount Gerizim. Jews and Samaritans were bitter rivals.
b: The Samaritans, who lived between Galilee and Judea, saw themselves as the heirs of the northern tribes and kept the five books of Moses, but worshiped at Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem (John 4:20). The Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple about 110 BC, and hostility ran both ways (Luke 9:52–54; John 4:9). This is the only mention of Samaritans in Matthew. Luke and John give them a large place (the good Samaritan, the woman at the well), and Acts 8 describes the gospel reaching Samaria soon after the resurrection, as Acts 1:8 foretells.

a: the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost
p: The prophets called Israel lost sheep, scattered by bad shepherds. Jesus sends the Twelve to find them.
b: "Lost sheep, that is what my people have been. Their shepherds made them stray" (Jeremiah 50:6). In Ezekiel 34 God promises to search for the lost himself (Ezekiel 34:11–16). The phrase probably means all Israel, seen as lost, not only the obvious sinners within it; the crowds were "like sheep that have no shepherd" (9:36). The parable of the lost sheep (18:12–14) carries the same image to Matthew's church.

p: The Twelve are sent to do exactly what Jesus has just done in chapters 8–9.
b: Every task in this verse matches a deed in chapters 8–9: healing the sick (8:5–17; 9:2–8), raising the dead (9:18–26), cleansing skin disease (8:1–4) and driving out demons (8:28–34; 9:32–34). Their message is his too: "the kingdom of heaven has drawn near" (4:17; 10:7). Jesus' answer to John the Baptist lists the same signs (11:5). The disciples share his authority (10:1), and in this chapter they will share his rejection (10:24–25).

a: You received for free, so give for free
p: Jewish teachers were urged not to profit from the Torah. Early churches tested preachers by their greed.
b: The healing and the message were gifts, so the messengers may not sell them. Jewish sages taught the same about the Torah: Hillel warned that "one who makes worldly use of the crown" of learning will perish (Mishnah Avot 1:13), and Rabbi Zadok said not to make the Torah "a spade to dig with" (Mishnah Avot 4:5); most rabbis earned their living by a trade. The Didache says a traveling prophet who asks for money is a false prophet (Didache 11:6, 12). Yet the next verses add that a worker deserves his food (10:10).

p: Mark lets the Twelve take a staff and sandals. Matthew and Luke forbid a staff. Why?
b: Mark 6:8–9 allows "only a staff" and sandals. Luke 9:3 forbids a staff; Matthew forbids sandals and staff. Answers: (1) Matthew's verb in 10:9 is "get" or "acquire" (ktaomai): do not go out and obtain extra supplies, but go as you are. (2) The sayings came down in more than one form, and each Gospel kept a version. (3) The aim is the same in all: total dependence on God and on the hospitality of those who receive them. Some scholars compare Cynic philosophers who wandered with cloak, bag and staff; the Twelve are to carry even less. Later, Jesus loosens the rule for a new situation (Luke 22:35–36).

a: A worker has earned his food
p: Paul calls this a command of the Lord, and 1 Timothy quotes it beside the Law of Moses.
b: Luke has "wages" instead of "food" (Luke 10:7). Paul refers to it: "the Lord gave an order that those who announce the good news are to live from the good news" (1 Corinthians 9:14), though he chose not to use the right. 1 Timothy 5:18 quotes Luke's form next to Deuteronomy 25:4 ("Do not muzzle an ox"), calling both "Scripture." The Didache applies it to true prophets and teachers (Didache 13:1–2). Matthew's "food" fits messengers who are given meals, not money.

a: let your peace settle on it
p: "Peace" (shalom) was the normal greeting, but here it acts like a blessing that can land or come back.
b: The greeting "Peace to you" (Hebrew shalom) was ordinary. Jesus treats it as a real gift that rests on a worthy house or returns to the giver, like God's word, which does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11). Luke speaks of a "son of peace" in the house (Luke 10:5–6). "Worthy" here means open to the messengers and their message, not morally superior.

a: shake its dust off your feet
p: A public sign of breaking ties: we take nothing from you, and you answer for yourselves.
b: Paul and Barnabas did this when driven out of Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51), and Paul shook out his clothes at Corinth (Acts 18:6). Many commentators connect it with the idea that the soil of Gentile lands was unclean, so that Jews coming home might shake it off; the evidence for such a custom is late and thin. Either way the meaning is clear: a town that rejects God's messengers is treated as outside the people of God, and the responsibility is now theirs.
r: Acts 13:51; Acts 18:6; Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5; Luke 10:10–11; Nehemiah 5:13

a: the land of Sodom and Gomorrah
p: Sodom was the byword for judgment. In Jewish tradition its sin included cruelty to strangers.
b: Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed by fire (Genesis 19:24–25) and became a proverb for God's judgment (Isaiah 1:9; Jude 1:7). The prophets and later Jewish writers named many sins: pride and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49), sexual crimes, and above all the mob's attack on Lot's guests. The Wisdom of Solomon says Sodom was punished for refusing to welcome strangers (Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–15). That makes the comparison sharp: a town that refuses Jesus' messengers is worse off than Sodom, which at least never heard them. Jesus says the same of Capernaum (11:23–24).
r: Genesis 19:1–25; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Isaiah 1:9; Jude 1:7; Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–15; 11:23–24; Luke 10:12

a: be sharp like snakes and pure like doves
p: Phronimos is the word for the serpent in Eden. Akeraios means "unmixed," with no hidden motive.
b: The Greek Old Testament calls the serpent of Genesis 3:1 the most phronimos, "shrewd," of the animals. Jesus borrows the snake's caution without its malice. Akeraios means pure, unmixed, without guile (Romans 16:19; Philippians 2:15). The dove could stand for silliness (Hosea 7:11), but here it means harmlessness. A later Jewish midrash says something close: toward God Israel is innocent as doves, and among the nations shrewd as serpents (Song of Songs Rabbah 2:14). Being "sheep" among "wolves" means the messengers cannot fight back; they must be wise and blameless.

p: Local Jewish courts could punish members with thirty-nine lashes. "Their" shows Matthew's distance.
b: The "councils" (synedria) were local Jewish courts. The Law limited a flogging to forty strokes (Deuteronomy 25:2–3), and the Mishnah gives the practice of thirty-nine (Mishnah Makkot 3:10–12). Paul received it five times (2 Corinthians 11:24), and once dealt it out to believers himself (Acts 22:19). Such punishment shows that the first Jewish believers were still inside the synagogue's discipline: courts discipline members, not outsiders. Matthew speaks of "their synagogues" (4:23; 9:35; 12:9; 13:54; 23:34), which suggests that by his time his church met apart. The verse describes a painful quarrel inside a family, not Jews as such.
r: Deuteronomy 25:2–3; 2 Corinthians 11:24; Acts 5:40; Acts 22:19; 23:34; Mark 13:9; Luke 21:12

t: A mission discourse with a future
p: The Twelve's short trip to Galilee's towns did not bring them before kings. Matthew looks further ahead.
b: Much of 10:17–22 appears in Mark's speech about the end (Mark 13:9–13). Matthew moved it here, so the mission speech covers the whole time until the Son of Man comes (10:23). In Acts the apostles did stand before Roman governors and Jewish kings: Peter and John before the council (Acts 4), James killed by Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:1–2), Paul before Felix, Festus and Agrippa II (Acts 24–26). Traditional readers see prophecy; critical scholars see the experience of the church in Matthew's day written into Jesus' charge. Either way, the first readers knew these were not empty warnings.

p: A phrase found only here. Luke has "the Holy Spirit" and, elsewhere, "I will give you a mouth."
b: Luke's parallels say the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say (Luke 12:12), or that Jesus will give them words no opponent can resist (Luke 21:15). Matthew's phrase links the Spirit to God as "your Father," the name Jesus has taught them to pray (6:9). Acts shows it happening: Peter "filled with the Holy Spirit" before the council (Acts 4:8), and Stephen's opponents "no match for the wisdom and the Spirit he spoke with" (Acts 6:10). The promise is for times of trial, not an excuse for not preparing to teach.

a: whoever holds out to the end, that person will be saved
p: Does this mean only those who endure were truly saved, or that a believer can fall away?
b: The saying returns in 24:13. "The end" may mean the end of a person's life, the end of the age, or the end of the persecution. Christians read the promise differently. In Reformed teaching those whom God has truly saved will persevere, so endurance is the mark of real faith (Westminster Confession 17). Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and many other readers take it as a real warning: one can fall away, and endurance, by grace, matters to final salvation. Both agree it is meant to encourage persecuted believers to hold on.

a: until the Son of Man comes
p: One of the hardest verses in Matthew. Did Jesus expect the end before the Twelve finished their mission?
b: Readings: (1) Mistaken expectation: Albert Schweitzer (1906) made this verse central, arguing Jesus expected the end before the Twelve came back and was disappointed. (2) The resurrection or Pentecost: the Son of Man "comes" in vindication soon after. (3) AD 70: the coming is judgment on Jerusalem, within that generation (R. T. France; preterist readers). (4) The second coming, with a continuing mission to Israel: the mission to the Jewish people will not be finished before he returns (many futurist and some Catholic readers). (5) Dispensationalists often see a future Jewish witness in the tribulation. See the chapter page.

p: A name for Satan. It plays on "head of the house." The KJV's "Beelzebub" comes from the Latin.
b: Baal-zebub, "lord of flies," was the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), perhaps a mocking change of Baal-zebul, "Baal the prince" or "lord of the exalted house" (zebul, dwelling, 1 Kings 8:13). In Jesus' day Beelzebul was a name for the ruler of demons (12:24). Jesus plays on it: if they call the "head of the house" (oikodespotēs) "lord of the house," they will slander his household too. The Greek manuscripts read Beelzeboul (Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus have Beezeboul); "Beelzebub" came into English from the Latin Vulgate. Matthew has set this up in 9:34.

a: fear the One who can destroy soul and body alike in Gehenna
p: Fear God, not human killers. Whether "destroy" means endless punishment or ending is debated.
b: "The One" is God, the only judge who decides beyond death (most readers; a few have thought of the devil). Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, had become a name for the place of final judgment (see the note at 5:22). Jewish martyr stories used the same contrast: the Maccabean brothers urged one another not to fear the one who thinks he kills, since the soul faces a far greater danger (4 Maccabees 13:14–15). "Destroy" (apollymi) is read in two ways: (1) ruin in endless punishment (the majority tradition, with 25:46); (2) final destruction, ending existence (conditional immortality: Edward Fudge, John Stott tentatively, Adventists). See the card on this chapter.

p: English Bibles add "will," "knowledge" or "care." The Greek says only "without your Father."
b: The Greek aneu tou patros hymōn leaves the meaning open: not without his knowing, his permitting, or his presence. Translators supply a word. The point is from the lesser to the greater: if God attends to sparrows sold two for a cheap coin (Luke 12:6 has five for two coins), he cares far more for his children. The comfort here is not that disciples will not die (10:28) but that nothing happens to them outside the Father's reach.
orig: ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν (aneu tou patros hymōn)

p: Homologeō is to declare publicly, as before a court. Peter later "denies" Jesus with the same verb.
b: "Declare for me" is literally "confess in me," an Aramaic way of saying "acknowledge me." The setting is the trials of 10:17–20: when asked, will the disciple stand with Jesus? Jesus promises to stand with that person before God the judge. "Deny" (arneomai) is the verb Matthew uses for Peter's denials in the high priest's courtyard (26:70, 72), and yet Peter was restored. Later Christian martyr stories turn on this verse: to say "I am a Christian" before a magistrate was to confess; to curse Christ was to deny.

a: I did not come to cast peace, but a sword
p: The sword here is division, as Luke's version says. It is not a call to violence.
b: Luke's parallel says "division" (Luke 12:51), and the next verses explain: families will split over Jesus. The Messiah was expected to bring peace (Isaiah 9:6–7; Zechariah 9:10), and Jesus blesses peacemakers (5:9) and tells Peter to put away his sword (26:52). But peace with God does not mean peace with everyone, and his coming forces a choice that divides. Simeon told Mary that a sword would pierce her own soul (Luke 2:34–35). The verse has sometimes been quoted to justify religious violence, which nothing in the context supports.
orig: οὐκ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην ἀλλὰ μάχαιραν (ouk ēlthon balein eirēnēn alla machairan)

a: I came to set a man at odds with his father
t: Micah 7:6 and the troubles before the Messiah
p: Jesus applies Micah's picture of a broken society to the families of his followers.
b: Micah 7:6 laments a time when a son treats his father with contempt, a daughter rises against her mother and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are his own household. Jewish tradition read it as a sign of the last days: the Mishnah lists it among the troubles "in the footsteps of the Messiah" (Mishnah Sotah 9:15), and Jubilees 23:16 also pictures children against parents. Jesus uses it of the strife his message will cause (see 10:21). For Jewish believers in Matthew's day it described a real cost: households split over Jesus.
r: Micah 7:6; 10:21; Mishnah Sotah 9:15; Jubilees 23:16; Luke 12:52–53; Malachi 4:6; Luke 1:17

t: The first mention of the cross
p: Before Jesus says anything about his own death, he tells disciples to take up a cross.
b: Every Galilean knew what this meant. When rebels rose after Herod the Great died in 4 BC, the Roman governor Varus crucified two thousand men (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 17.295). A condemned man usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution; Plutarch remarks, in his essay On the Delays of the Divine Vengeance, that every criminal who goes to execution carries his own cross. So the saying means: be ready for shame and death for my sake. Here it comes before Jesus foretells his death (16:21); it returns more fully in 16:24, after that.

t: Life and soul are one word
p: Psychē means life, self or soul. It is the same word as "soul" in 10:28.
b: Greek psychē covers the physical life, the self and the soul. Jesus plays on its range: the one who "finds" his life, saving himself by denying Jesus under pressure, loses his true life; the one who loses his life for Jesus, even to death, finds it. The saying appears six times in the Gospels in different forms (16:25; Mark 8:35; Luke 9:24; Luke 17:33; John 12:25), which shows how deeply it marked the early church.

a: Whoever takes you in takes me in
p: The sent one stands for the sender. Matthew 25 builds on the same idea.
b: This is the agent principle (see the note at 10:2): the messenger carries the authority of the one who sent him (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). To give the Twelve a home was to welcome Jesus, and through him God. The same chain appears in 18:5 (welcoming a child), John 13:20, and at the end of Jesus' teaching in the judgment of the nations, where what is done for "one of these brothers of mine, even the least of them" is done for him (25:40). Hospitality to the traveling preachers was how most early churches began.

a: in the name of a prophet
p: "In the name of" means "because he is." Matthew's church had traveling prophets.
b: Eis onoma is a Hebrew way of saying "for the sake of" or "as." To take in a prophet because he is a prophet is to share in his work and reward. Christian prophets were active in Matthew's day (7:15–23; 23:34; Acts 11:27; 13:1), and the Didache gives rules for receiving them (Didache 11–13). The "righteous" may be faithful believers generally, or a recognized group. In the Old Testament the widow who sheltered Elijah and the woman who made a room for Elisha received a prophet's reward (1 Kings 17:8–24; 2 Kings 4:8–37).

p: In Matthew "little ones" are Jesus' disciples, ordinary believers. This matters for reading 25:40.
b: Jesus calls his disciples "little ones" again in 18:6, 10 and 14. Here "one of these little ones" is explained by "in the name of a disciple." So the smallest kindness to the humblest disciple will be rewarded. Many interpreters use this verse to read the parable of the sheep and goats: "these brothers of mine, even the least of them" (25:40) would be Jesus' followers, especially his messengers. Others read 25:40 as all the poor and needy. The two readings shape very different ideas of what Jesus asks.
